author: Alex
body:
Thanks for the informative post! One note is that for negative numbers modulo may work differently than one expects, as the rule " if a is less than n then a % n always equals a" doesn't hold. Here is the output of a C program:

-4 % 2 is 0
-3 % 2 is -1
-2 % 2 is 0
-1 % 2 is -1
0 % 2 is 0
1 % 2 is 1
2 % 2 is 0
3 % 2 is 1
4 % 2 is 0

author: Federico Hatoum
body: And thank you also, Alex, for your value-added comments. I've edited the quote from the WatchHogStories blog to specify that the "a" value must be positive.

author: Jeremy J
body:
I'm extremely facinated by the math/programming behind slot machines in casinos. One of the major aspects of slot machines is the use of the modulo operator.

For example, a single virtual reel in a slot machine might have 128 different stops numbered 0-127. The RNG is the machine is spitting out huge random numbers every microsecond. When one of these numbers is grabbed it will use modulo operator to determine the 0-127 result from that massive number.

author: Federico Hatoum
body:
Sure, you could use a loop and increment with +4. Using modulo is, in my opinion, cleaner and easier to read.
For example, with modulo you can test if an index is safe without needing to loop through all of the previous choices. If you were testing if index 2 was a safe place to start with a loop, you'd have to have logic in your loop to check when you arrived at step 2 (of a 4 increment loop) and test its "safety". With modulo you do that all in one step, without looping.

author: Suresh
body: can you tell why modulo is used in some implementation of hashmap (specifically in Java) to determine the size of the bucket i.e array of key/value pairs.

author: Federico Hatoum
body:
Hi Suresh. I wasn't familiar with how modulo is used in HashMap, so I did some searching and think I now understand.
From what I read, HashMaps have Nodes which are the entries and each node goes into a Bucket.

The Bucket that a Node goes into is determined by the modulo of the hash value and the capacity of the HashMap.
